payload.title: Ideal external gear pair

model.title: Ideal external gear pair
model.description: Unqualified teaching proposal for human review: tooth-count ratio determines steady rotational speed and direction in two externally meshing gears.
assumptions: Adjustable illustrative defaults: driving frequency 0.5 Hz, driving tooth count 20, driven tooth count 40.
Driving frequency is restricted to 0.1–2 Hz. Each tooth-count control selects only 20, 30, or 40 teeth.
Both gears are rigid external spur gears on fixed parallel shafts, with compatible involute geometry and continuous ideal engagement.
Illustrative geometry: module 0.004 m, pressure angle 0.3490658503988659 radians, addendum 0.004 m, dedendum 0.005 m. These are teaching choices, not measured specifications.
Shafts point along z. The driving centre is the origin; the driven centre lies on +x at the calculated centre distance. Positive rotation is counterclockwise viewed from +z.
Driving rotation is positive. Signed cyclic frequencies drive continuous rotation on Play; angular velocities are separately calculated in radians per second.
At zero rotation, a driving tooth points toward +x. The driven phase offset places a gap toward the driving gear for these even tooth counts.
Steady model: time_experiment=null. No clock or transient response is needed for continuous rotation.
Guided comparisons use 20 driving 40 teeth, 40 driving 20 teeth, and 30 driving 30 teeth at the same driving frequency.
limitations: Ideal steady kinematics only; excludes torque, power, friction, backlash, tooth stresses, acceleration dynamics, and other gear arrangements.
Tooth contact explains equal tooth-passing rates; contact forces and deformation are not calculated.
Toothed geometry is a simplified teaching representation, not a manufacturing design or engineering validation.
Changing controls replaces the steady configuration immediately; assembly adjustment and engagement transients are not simulated.

nodes.description: Teeth passing the mesh per second, equal for both gears; bounded 2–80 Hz.

nodes.description: Pitch radius times pressure-angle cosine; bounded 0.03758–0.07518 m.

nodes.description: Pitch radius times pressure-angle cosine; bounded 0.03758–0.07518 m.

nodes.label: Speed reduction
nodes.description: 1 when driven speed magnitude is smaller; otherwise 0.

nodes.label: Speed increase
nodes.description: 1 when driven speed magnitude is larger; otherwise 0.

nodes.description: Sum of mutually exclusive reduction and increase flags; 0 or 1.

nodes.description: 1 only for equal tooth counts; otherwise 0.

nodes.label: Nonreduction mode
nodes.description: Intermediate mode: 2 for increase, 1 otherwise.

nodes.label: Transmission mode
nodes.description: Shared explanatory mode: 0 reduction, 1 equal speed, 2 increase. Bind explanations to this same state.

limits: Ideal steady kinematics only; excludes torque, power, friction, backlash, tooth stresses, acceleration dynamics and other gear arrangements.
Contact forces and deformation are not calculated. This teaching representation is not a manufacturing design or engineering validation.
Driving frequency is 0.1–2 Hz; each tooth count selects only 20, 30 or 40. Illustrative defaults are 0.5 Hz and 20 driving 40 teeth.
One metre maps to 100 scene units on every axis; physical equations retain SI values. The driving shaft centre is the physical origin.

parts.label: Base
parts.explanation: This heavy plate supports both shafts and keeps the gears upright.

parts.label: Base mounting bolts
parts.explanation: These bolts anchor the base at its corners.

parts.label: Driving shaft assembly
parts.explanation: The driving assembly supplies the input rotation.

parts.label: Driving rear support
parts.explanation: This sturdy support holds a bearing around the driving shaft.

parts.label: Driving rear bearing
parts.explanation: A bearing supports a turning shaft with balls between two rings.

parts.label: Driving rear bearing cover
parts.explanation: This removable ring keeps the bearing seated while leaving room for the shaft.

parts.label: Driving front support
parts.explanation: This support holds the other end of the driving shaft level.

parts.label: Driving front bearing
parts.explanation: Its central opening fits the shaft, while the outer ring sits in the support.

parts.label: Driving front bearing cover
parts.explanation: Remove this cover to see the bearing inside its support.

parts.label: Driving cover screws
parts.explanation: These screws secure the two bearing covers to their supports.

parts.label: Driving rotating assembly
parts.explanation: The shaft, hub and driving gear turn together.

parts.label: Driving shaft
parts.explanation: This shaft carries input rotation to the driving gear.

parts.label: Driving gear
parts.explanation: Its teeth meet gaps in the driven gear, making that gear turn the other way.

parts.label: Driving gear hub
parts.explanation: The hub is the thick central fitting that joins the gear to its shaft.

parts.label: Driving shaft collar
parts.explanation: This ring helps keep the shaft from sliding through its bearings.

parts.label: Driven shaft assembly
parts.explanation: The output assembly receives rotation from the driving gear.

parts.label: Driven rear support
parts.explanation: This support holds a bearing around the output shaft.

parts.label: Driven rear bearing
parts.explanation: The bearing supports the output shaft while allowing it to turn.

parts.label: Driven rear bearing cover
parts.explanation: This open-centred cover holds the bearing in its support.

parts.label: Driven front support
parts.explanation: This support keeps the output shaft parallel to the input shaft.

parts.label: Driven front bearing
parts.explanation: Two rings and a row of balls support the shaft inside this bearing.

parts.label: Driven front bearing cover
parts.explanation: Remove this ring to look into the output bearing support.

parts.label: Driven cover screws
parts.explanation: These screws hold the output bearing covers in place.

parts.label: Driven rotating assembly
parts.explanation: The output gear, hub and shaft turn together, opposite to the input.

parts.label: Driven shaft
parts.explanation: This shaft turns with the output gear.

parts.label: Driven gear
parts.explanation: A gear with more teeth needs more tooth contacts for one full turn. With the same teeth passing each second, it turns more slowly.

parts.label: Driven gear hub
parts.explanation: This central fitting connects the output gear to its shaft.

parts.label: Driven shaft collar
parts.explanation: This ring helps keep the output shaft in place along its length.

experiments.title: Follow the driving teeth.
experiments.prompt: Keep 20 driving 40 teeth. Predict what happens when input frequency changes from 0.5 to 1 Hz. Press Play, change it, and compare both gears.
experiments.explanation: The driving gear supplies rotation through contacting teeth. Increasing input frequency increases tooth-passing frequency and both rotational speeds without changing their ratio. Playback is slowed tenfold; readouts retain physical values.

experiments.title: Small gear drives large gear.
experiments.prompt: Set input frequency to 0.5 Hz and driving teeth to 20. Start with 20 driven teeth. Predict the output speed, then change driven teeth to 40 and compare.
experiments.explanation: The larger driven gear needs more tooth contacts per revolution. Equal tooth-passing rates therefore give a smaller output speed magnitude. The negative output frequency indicates opposite rotation viewed from +Z.

experiments.title: Large gear drives small gear.
experiments.prompt: Keep input frequency at 0.5 Hz. Set driven teeth to 20 and driving teeth to 20. Predict the effect of changing driving teeth to 40, then observe and compare.
experiments.explanation: More driving teeth pass the mesh per input revolution. The smaller driven gear completes more revolutions, so the speed magnitude ratio exceeds one. External meshing still reverses direction.

experiments.title: Match the tooth counts.
experiments.prompt: Keep input frequency at 0.5 Hz. Set driving teeth to 30 and driven teeth to 40. Predict what changes when driven teeth become 30, then compare motion and ratio.
experiments.explanation: Matching tooth counts give equal speed magnitudes, but opposite rotation directions. Configuration changes replace the steady geometry immediately; adjustment dynamics are not simulated. Inspection separation is not physical operating motion. This ideal teaching model excludes torque, power, friction, backlash, tooth stresses and acceleration dynamics; it is not engineering validation.

controls.help: Changes both gears' rotational speeds and the tooth-passing rate without changing the speed ratio.
Changes driving gear size, shaft spacing, tooth-passing rate and driven speed at fixed input frequency.
Changes driven gear size and shaft spacing; more driven teeth reduce output speed magnitude at fixed driving settings.

coverage.explanation: Input frequency and driving tooth count determine tooth-passing rate and output frequency. Inspect the driving teeth meeting driven gaps during signed-frequency playback; contact forces are not calculated.
Both tooth counts determine the speed ratio and driven angular velocity. The same controls regenerate gear sizes and set compatible shaft spacing.

Signed angular velocities establish opposite rotation. Compare 20 driving 40 teeth, 40 driving 20 teeth and 30 driving 30 teeth at the same input frequency to distinguish reduction, increase and equal-speed transmission.

outcomes: Identify the driving and driven gears and explain how contacting teeth transfer rotation.
Predict how the driven gear’s speed changes when its tooth count changes relative to the driving gear.
Observe that two externally meshing gears rotate in opposite directions and distinguish speed reduction, equal-speed transmission, and speed increase.

generation_quality.scope: Recipe, label, connection and dependency checks only. Dependency paths do not prove numeric change. Overlap, recognizability, physical correctness and child usability require separate evaluation.

visual.scope: Eight fitted views; projected bounds, center-ray occlusion, conservative bounding-box overlaps and estimated two-line label capacity. These heuristics do not replace rendered-image or child usability review.

sampled_quality.scope: Defaults, five points per input plus presets, a midpoint context for apparently inactive controls, all-input endpoints, and lesson experiments. Finite geometry and observed changes only; no proof of scientific accuracy, recognizability or complete state-space coverage.
